Rung with the bells half muffled to mark the anniversary of the death of The Right Honourable Frederick John Robinson, first Earl of Ripon, who died on 28th January 1859.

Lord Ripon lived at Nocton Hall and owned the Nocton Estate. All Saints Church was built as a memorial to Lord Ripon and the peal of six bells were given by his wife Lady Sarah Albinia Louisa, Countess of Ripon in 1865 in memory of him.
He was a former Chancellor of the Exchequer as well as a former Prime Minster, and is buried in the family vault here under All Saints.

Rung on twelfth night marking the end of Christmas and also celebrating the new year on Tennyson’s ‘Wild Bells’
‘Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky, The flying cloud, the frosty light: The year is dying in the night; Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.’
‘Ring out the old, ring in the new; Ring, happy bells, across the snow; The year is going, let him go; Ring out the false, ring in the true.’

These bells are thought to be the ‘Wild Bells’ from Tennyson’s poem ‘Ring Out, Wild Bells’. They originally hung at Hagworthingham just 2 miles south of Somersby and we know that Hagworthingham ringers were the active ringers in this area during the 1800s. They were transferred to Welbourn in 1978 after the tower collapsed at Hagworthingham. If you have rung on the bells at Welbourn their 'wild' tuning is also fitting for them being the 'Wild Bells' which Tennyson heard and inspired him!

It is thought that during his early years of living at Somersby he was inspired by the sound of Church bells which he could hear from his home in Somersby, with Hagworthingham being 2 miles away (became 8 in 1824), which resulted in him writing ‘Ring Out Wild Bells’ which is part of ‘In Memoriam’ which he started in 1834 whilst at Somersby.

The tenor bell at the Civic Church tolled as a mark of respect and in memory of Patrick The Right Honourable The Lord Cormack who passed away earlier today aged 84.

Lord Cormack lived in the City in Minster Yard, in the shadow of the Cathedral where he worshiped regularly, and was born in Grimsby making him a true yellowbelly ‘yellerbelly’. He was a great benefactor and supporter of the City and in recognition of this he was awarded the Freedom of the City of Lincoln by the Mayor at the City Guildhall in March 2022.

He was a devout Christian, undertaking the office of Rector’s Warden at the Parliamentary Parish Church of St Margaret’s Westminster 1978-1990, was Vice President of the National Churches Trust for over 40 years, was a member of the General Synod 1995-2005, served on the Ecclesiastical Committee of Parliament, was Deputy High Steward of Lincoln Cathedral and was President of the Prayer Book Society.

He was a keen historian and was highly involved in the building of the new Magna Carta Vault at Lincoln Castle and was Patron of the newly built International Bomber Command Memorial & Centre which stands overlooking the City.
A true Parliamentarian having served as an MP for 40 years before becoming an active life peer in the House of Lord’s since 2010.
'Well done, thou good and faithful servant'
From Lord Cormack’s speech accepting his Freedom of the City of Lincoln:

“I have had four red letter days in my public life; first when I was elected as an MP, secondly when I was given a knighthood, then when I accepted my seat in the House of Lords, and lastly today [being granted the Freedom of the City of Lincoln]."

“Of those four days, this is the most intimate, moving and special. I am indeed a Lincolnshire yellowbelly who is proud of our county and every day I look at that glorious cathedral, which I first saw in 1946 when my parents brought me from Grimsby to see it.”

Rung with the bells half muffled at the Civic Church on behalf of the Mayor & Civic Party as a mark of respect and in memory of The Right Honourable Patrick Thomas, The Lord Cormack who passed away on 25th February aged 84, and whose funeral is taking place this afternoon at Lincoln Cathedral.

Lord Cormack lived in the City in Minster Yard, in the shadow of the Cathedral where he worshiped regularly, and was born in Grimsby making him a true yellowbelly ‘yellerbelly’. He was a great benefactor and supporter of the City and in recognition of this he was awarded the Freedom of the City of Lincoln by the Mayor at the City Guildhall in March 2022.

He was a devout Christian, undertaking the office of Rector’s Warden at the Parliamentary Parish Church of St Margaret’s Westminster 1978-1990, was Vice President of the National Churches Trust for over 40 years, was a member of the General Synod 1995-2005, served on the Ecclesiastical Committee of Parliament, was Deputy High Steward of Lincoln Cathedral and was President of the Prayer Book Society.

He was a keen historian and was highly involved in the building of the new Magna Carta Vault at Lincoln Castle and was Patron of the newly built International Bomber Command Memorial & Centre which stands overlooking the City.
A true Parliamentarian having served as an MP for 40 years before becoming an active life peer in the House of Lord’s since 2010.
'Well done, thou good and faithful servant'
From Lord Cormack’s speech accepting his Freedom of the City of Lincoln:

“I have had four red letter days in my public life; first when I was elected as an MP, secondly when I was given a knighthood, then when I accepted my seat in the House of Lords, and lastly today [being granted the Freedom of the City of Lincoln]."

“Of those four days, this is the most intimate, moving and special. I am indeed a Lincolnshire yellowbelly who is proud of our county and every day I look at that glorious cathedral, which I first saw in 1946 when my parents brought me from Grimsby to see it.”

The Annual Culfrey Ringing.

Rung on the back three (the original three) on Lady Day to mark the end of the ringing of the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) each evening at 7pm between Michaelmas Day & Lady Day, a local tradition dating back to the seventeenth century to help guide lost travellers off the heath to the safety of the village.
The bells were rung up to 7pm, after which the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) was rung for 5 mins.
Due to it being Lent the bells were fully muffled but the tenor's backstroke muffle was removed so the culfrey bell could be heard tolling.

The Culfrey Trust still provide new bell ropes for the Culfrey Bell, upkeep the Church clock which took over the ringing of the bell, and provide two bungalows for elder parishioners called the Culfrey Bungalows on the site of the old Culfrey Cottages.

Remembering Frederick W Stokes of Blankney, who is the longest serving Secretary of the Lincoln Diocesan Guild, 1921 - 1950. Fred took part in many of the Guild's early ringing achievements such as the first peal on the new twelve at Lincoln Cathedral in 1929, being the first peal of Maximus rung for the Guild and in the County - Cambridge S Maximus by an all resident Guild band, and the first peal of London S Major rung for the Guild and in the County at Washingborough in 1928 to name but a few. However he was a grass roots ringer too, teaching many local bands and calling many first peals at various towers!
Blankney is the Guild’s overall fourth leading peal tower. It is the leading six bell peal tower with 236 peals rung for the Guild out of the 260 peals rung on the bells.

The conductor learnt to ring and joined the Guild 25 years ago during the Guild’s Centenary year 1999. Rung remembering Geoffrey R Parker, eighth Master of the Guild, 1992 – 2002, who was Master at that time (25 years ago). Geoff is the leading peal ringer here at Blankney having rung 81 peals on the bells, with the conductor being the second leading peal ringer here with 68. Geoff is the Guild’s second leading peal ringer having rung 1,548 peals for the Guild

Rung also remembering Jack L Millhouse, sixth Master of the Guild, 1982 – 1987 and also Secretary of the Guild, 1969 - 1974. Jack probably did more for Lincolnshire ringing and ringers than anyone else prior or previous to him, through encouraging, teaching and providing opportunities. He is the Guild’s leading peal ringer having rung 1,578 peals for the Guild, and Blankney is his leading six bell peal tower with 46 peals.

The Traditional Death Knell & Nine Tailors were tolled on the tenor bell (three lots of three for the Nine Tailors followed by 95 tolls representing the deceased’s age) as a mark of respect and in memory of George Ashton, former Churchwarden here at the Civic Church, on the morning of his funeral.
Rung open in celebration of the life of George Ashton, immediately prior to his funeral here at this Church.

George was highly respected within Lincoln, volunteering for various things across the City, but especially in connection to Lincoln City Football Club 'The Imps', the Lincoln Branch of the Conservative Association, and here at St Peter-at-Gowts and at the Civic Church of St Mary-le-Wigford.

George was made Life President of the Lincoln Branch of the Conservative Association and was actively involved with the Conservatives all his life. He met all the Conservative leaders since Winston Churchill and was pleased to meet Rishi Sunak last December just before Christmas when he visited George in his care home.

George was a big supporter of Lincoln City Football Club 'The Imps', attending matches with his beloved wife Doreen – they were both club legends in their own right, a true double act! Since attending his first match in 1934 George only missed 6 home matches in 80 years up until Covid.
Whilst we rang the quarter peal the funeral cortege did a lap of Sincil Bank (home of the Imps) where fans and staff made a guard of honour before it made its way the short distance to the Church.

George was a past Churchwarden here at this Church where he married his beloved Doreen in 1952, but later on at the Civic Church of St Mary-le-Wigford - where supported by his wife Doreen, they tirelessly kept St Mary's open and functioning, and where they are both fondly remembered. At today’s service the conductor – the current Churchwarden at the Civic Church, laid his Churchwarden’s staff on top of George’s coffin.
George sadly passed away on 12th May 2024 aged 95. RIP George, now reunited with your beloved Doreen.

Rung prior to the Civic Service on Restoration Day to welcome the new Mayor to Office - the 819th Mayor of Lincoln.

Today marks the 364th anniversary of the Restoration of the Monarchy in 1660 - known as Royal Oak Day. It is most fitting that we were welcoming the new Mayor and Sheriff to Office on this anniversary with the close links and connections that both the City and the Office of Mayor holds with the Crown and Monarchy.

The City’s Great Mace - 'which is to be carried before the Mayor', was given by King Charles I, whose coat of arms adorn it, it being given in October 1640 when Charles I was making his way back up to London for the Long Parliament. To mark the restoration in 1660 the Mace was further embellished with the addition of a crown, orb and cross being placed on top of it along with the coat of arms of King Charles II.

Today's Civic Service took the form of Holy Communion according to the Book of Common Prayer (1662) with the additional Collects & Prayers for The Restoration - the twenty ninth day of May, used. The service was attended by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln - Councillor Alan Briggs, and the City Sheriff - Mr Brian Harding.
Also celebrating the recent news that His Majesty King Charles III has agreed to continue his Patronage of the Prayer Book Society.

And danced the skies on laughter-silvered wings;
Sunward I’ve climbed, and joined the tumbling mirth
of sun-split clouds, — and done a hundred things
You have not dreamed of – wheeled and soared and swung
High in the sunlit silence. Hov’ring there,
I’ve chased the shouting wind along, and flung
My eager craft through footless halls of air....
Up, up the long, delirious, burning blue
I’ve topped the wind-swept heights with easy grace.

The high untrespassed sanctity of space,

Rung by six local women to honour the 60th anniversary of Dale Greig becoming the first woman to run a marathon in under 3 hours 30 minutes, on 23rd May 1964. Her time of 3:27:45 at the Isle of Wight Marathon was recognised by the International Association of Athletics Federations as a world best. She was also the first woman to run a marathon in Britain.

Greig had to persuade the organisers to let her compete, and she was made to start four minutes ahead of the men. This meant that her run could be called a time trial, rather than a race against the men. Greig was followed round the course by an ambulance.

Major Stone landed early at Bernieres-sur-Mer on Juno Beach with the Royal Engineers in support of the Canadians. He was a Major in command of four Platoons, over 200 men across about a 3 mile front. Their initial task was to clear obstacles to create gaps for the landing craft. The water was much deeper than predicted. He jumped into the water to clear mines and was awarded a Distinguished Service Order (just one of 8 earned by an RE on the day). They then went on to clear mines and obstacles, and demolish and build bridges.

First inside - 2. Rung for national 'Ring Out for Peace on the 80th Anniversary of the D-Day Landings' commemoration. A particularly poignant event for Angela Elliott as her father, Gerald Lawrence Reginald Mumby, took part. She writes:

'Eighty years after D-Day we came together to commemorate the great sacrifice made by thousands of young men landing on the Normandy beaches on 6th June 1944, who died, and to celebrate the lives of those, like my father, who returned home, by ringing my first quarter peal on an inside bell to Plain Bob Doubles.

My father died in 2015, having reached the age of 90. Three weeks before his death France honoured him with the Legion D’Honneur for his part in the D-Day landings. He always said he didn’t do much. This was far from the truth. At three weeks short of 19, he was sent on secondment with the Dorset Regiment as a telegraphist/radio operator (he was actually in the Navy, but the Dorset's had run out of radio operators) to land on Gold Beach in the first wave of British troops. Making their way through the dead and dying, under mortar attack and sniper fire, and risking life and limb through the mines, he made his way into the dunes to dig in and act as a spotter for ship to shore forward bombardment. All in all he spent three weeks in France, complained about not changing his socks, worried for the French who had undergone severe deprivations and maltreatment by the enemy, and terrified out of his mind. When he returned to the UK he had a week’s leave before he was sent to Singapore for the Japanese surrender.

My brother, Robert Mumby (a non-ringer) was kind enough to bring Dad’s medals, including the Legion D’Honneur, to the tower today, so we could ring both for D-Day and also in my Dad’s memory - Gerald Lawrence Reginald Mumby 14th July 1925 – 23rd October 2015'.

The Civic Bells pealed out half muffled over the City during the Freedom Parade of RAF Waddington on the 80th anniversary of D-Day, as they exercised their right to parade/march through the City of Lincoln with Colours flying, bayonets fixed, bands playing and bells pealing. Marking the bases close connections to the City standing immediately to the south of the City.

Today’s Freedom Parade saw 150 personnel from RAF Waddington marching through the City marking the 65th anniversary of the granting of the Freedom of the City of Lincoln to RAF Waddington in 1959, on 25th April, and also commemorating the 80th anniversary of D-Day and the Normandy Landings to Liberate Europe during World War Two.

The parade was led by the RAF Waddington Pipes and Drums and was preceded by the Civic Procession which took place from the Guildhall down the High Street to the City War Memorial to wait for the parade to arrive.

The parade marched down the High Street from St Martin’s Square, passing the Guildhall to the City War Memorial, which stands 150 yards away from the Civic Church of St Mary le Wigford and within earshot of the bells, from where the bells could be clear heard pealing out over the parade. The parade came to a halt at the City War Memorial and a flypast took place.

The parade was inspected by His Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for the County of Lincolnshire, Mr Toby Dennis, and the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, Councillor Alan Briggs. Also present were the City Sheriff, members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party, the Freemen of the City and other City Dignitaries including the Churchwardens of the Civic Church. The official salute to His Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for Lincolnshire and to the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln was given before the Parade marched off to finish in City Square.

Christopher Woodcock, the Civic Ringing Master, wishes to be associated with this ringing but was unable to ring due to undertaking his Civic Churchwarden duties at the Freedom Parade, taking part in the Civic Procession.

A Tribute to Clare McNeil, 1976-2024.
Bell Ringer at St Mark’s Church, Bilton, for 14 Months.
It was with great sadness that Clare’s funeral took place at St Mark’s on 17th July 2024. A bell was tolled before the funeral, and we rang joyfully on 6 bells afterwards, as requested by the family.

Clare and her son Barnaby joined St Mark’s bell ringing team on August Bank Holiday Monday, 2022, as complete beginners. Clare soon became a treasured and enthusiastic member of the team, despite often being sceptical of her own natural ability.
Although only ringing for a few months, she was lucky enough to join in several national events:
. Ringing during the Period of Mourning for the death of HM Queen Elizabeth II and on the day of the subsequent State Funeral in September 2022.
. Joining in the huge national event Ring For The King in May 2023 to mark the Coronation of King Charles III.
. Joining Barnaby and family on a weekend in York in July 2023 for the annual Ringing World National Youth Contest, in which Barnaby was taking part as a member of Coventry Spires.
Ringing for HM Queen Elizabeth II and for King Charles III has earned Clare recognition on Bellboard, the Ringing World’s on-line record of church bell ringing nationally.

Clare and Barnaby retired from ringing in November 2023, due to pressures of Barnaby’s football matches and Clare’s now full-time job - this was sad, but fully understandable. At Bilton, Clare will be remembered as an always-cheerful, always-joyful member of the team.
David Price

P.S. Clare and her family have had a long-standing connection with St Mark’s, Bilton. Clare and Tom met in Kenya, where both were teachers, and they came back to St Mark’s to be married. In subsequent years, they taught in Kenya, Qatar and El Salvador. On the way, they had their son Barnaby and twins Robyn and Felix - they came back to England for the births, and the children were all Christened at St Mark’s. In 2022, they moved permanently back to Bilton. That’s an extremely brief rendering of Clare’s adventurous life, which was more fully recounted in the entertaining  tribute given at the funeral.

Rung in memory of Captain Matthew Flinders RN, native of neighbouring Donington - being born there on 16th March 1774, who is returning home today and is being reburied inside St Mary and the Holy Rood Church Donington - the Church where he was baptised. He is being given full Naval honours including an 18 gun salute and pallbearers from the Royal Navy's state ceremonial team.

The young Matthew Flinders was educated here at Horbling at the Reverend John Shinglar's Grammar School, which is thought to have been held in this Church - Rev Shinglar being the curate here and is named on the fourth bell.

Captain Flinders led the first circumnavigation of Australia, and is credited with naming the continent. He died in London on 19th July 1814 aged 40 and was buried in St James's burial ground Camden, until his lost grave was rediscovered in 2019.

This ringing followed a short re-dedication service performed by the Rector, Revd Garry Hinchcliffe, including the following blessing.
'Heavenly Father, We pray for these church bells and for those who have rung them past and present.
We remember their function historically as a call to those who came to market, and we remember their function today as a call to worship, a call to peace and a call to salvation.
May their sound at this moment of their rededication continue to enrich all our lives from the greatest to the least.
These things we ask and pray in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.'

The 21st September 2024 saw the 150th anniversary of the birth of Gustav Holst. Gustav was born in Cheltenham, Gloucestershire at No. 4 Pittville Terrace, now No. 4 Clarence Road. This is now a museum to Gustav's memory known as the 'Victorian House'.

To mark this anniversary a special commemorative service took place at St Botolph's Church, Bishopsgate in the City of London on Wednesday 18th September at 1.10pm. The service consisted of two voluntaries for organ which Gustav composed between 1890 and 1891. One was played at the beginning of the service and the other was played at the very end. We also had two hymns by Gustav as well as two sections from the mass by Imogen Holst, Gustav's only daughter.
Before the service a quarter peal of Plain Bob Triples was rung by members of the Wednesday Lunchtime band.

Special 90th Birthday Compliment to Derek C Jackson, who has been a member of the Eling band since 1963, and was Tower Captain from 2005 – 2017, when he reluctantly had to give up ringing due to ill health.

Among Derek’s many achievements over the years, he founded the Southampton University Guild of Change Ringers in 1954. He is particularly proud of this as the Guild is still thriving after 70 years and counting.

Derek was the Winchester & Portsmouth Diocesan Guild Secretary in the early 1970’s, where he was instrumental in setting up the Guild Bell Restoration Fund, he was again Guild Secretary in the 1980’s & 90’s.

Derek was a W&P Central Council Representative in the 1980’s & 90’s. He was also Christchurch & Southampton District Ringing Master for several years, and has conducted many peals, including peals of multiple Doubles methods some consisting of over 100 methods. Derek has been an inspiration to generations of ringers, including myself!

Rung to mark the 235th anniversary of the bells being cast by Thomas Osborn of Downham Market and officially opened and rung for the first time on 23rd October 1789.
The opening was recorded in the Norwich Journal dated 31st October 1789:

“On Friday last a new peal of six bells were opened at Timberland in the County of Lincoln by a society of ringers from Bicker in the said county with the peals of treble and court bob. After much good ringing on that day the gentlemen in the town and neighbourhood met at the Miller’s Arms where the evening was spent with the greatest harmony and satisfaction. The bells were cast and hung by Thomas Osborn of Downham in Norfolk and are allowed by capital Judges to be a very fine peal of bells.”

Rung in memory of all those who have lost their lives fighting for our Country in conflicts past and present, especially during the two World Wars, but especially the 12 men & boys from this village who lost their lives in the Great War and did not return, all of whom are commemorated on the Village War Memorial.
We especially remember Private WILLIAM HENRY ROSSINGTON who was killed in action on 15th April 1918 aged 21. William was a ringer at this Church.

Also Pioneer WILLIAM PEARSON GREEN who was killed in action on 28th June 1916 aged 25 and Private GEORGE HENRY COOKE who died of wounds on 20th December 1917 aged 29. William & George were both ringers at neighbouring Metheringham Church.

William & George rang their first 720 on 8th October 1912 at Metheringham, being Grandsire Doubles, conducted by Fred Stokes who was Tower Captain here at Blankney. https://bb.ringingworld.co.uk/view.php?id=1204050
We Will Remember Them!
When You Go Home, Tell Them Of Us And Say, For Your Tomorrow, We Gave Our Today.

The Service was attended by the Vice Lord-Lieutenant, the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff, the Chairman of the County Council, the City MP, members of the Civic Party and the Freemen of the City, along with various Forces Organisations, Associations, Veterans, Cadets and the various Standard Bearers, with music being led by the Lincolnshire Fire & Rescue Concert Band. Wreaths were laid by the Vice Lord-Lieutenant on behalf of the County followed by the Mayor of Lincoln and City Sheriff on behalf of the City. Following this wreaths were laid by the Royal British Legion and by representatives from each of the tri-services (Army, Royal Navy & Royal Air Force) followed by the Freemen of the City and various Forces Associations and Veterans.

As requested by Richard J Cann before he died, open ringing half-muffled before his funeral and unmuffled afterwards. Rounds and Queens on 12 were rung on handbells around his coffin by Jonathan Evans, Linda Armitage, Ros Fox, Rowena Shipley, Mike Dodson and Stephen Shipley during the service and a QP (see separate BellBoard entry) of his favourite composition of his favourite method (Grandsire Triples) was rung later the same afternoon on the back eight, thus including "Richard's bell" (the eleventh of the twelve).
Also present: Gillian M Stead, Helen Wallace.

Rung in thanksgiving for the life of Richard J Cann (1938-2024) and for his service to the church for many years, following his funeral. Richard was a ringer at this tower and a member of the St Alphege Guild and the St Martin's Guild for over 65 years. At St Alphege, he was Ringing Master (1991-1996) and also, at various times, Secretary, Treasurer, Church and Churchyard Representative, Tower Keeper, Handbell Treasurer and Handbell Leader.
His favourite composition of his favourite method, rung on the back eight to include "Richard's bell", the eleventh of the twelve.
Truly the end of an era.

For celebrating the following 3 occasions.

1. 200th anniversary of the augmentation of the bells at Longney from 6 to 8 by John Rudhall which were opened between 26th and 30th December 1824 most likely by the Longney band one of the two new treble bells the second was the gift of William Longney one of Longney's previous tower captain's, (Lionel Longney's) ancestors. It's most likely the reason for the augmentation of the bells at Longney was cause William Longney had learnt his eight bell ringing in Gloucester and wanted to do it at Longney. So he decided to get the bells there augmented from 6 to 8. The treble bell was funded by public subscription whilst the second bell was the gift of himself at which it has his name inscribed on it making the bell easily refereed to as the Longney special bell.

2. 150th anniversary of the erection of the church clock which was erected December 1873 to January 1874 so this quarter was also rung as a belated 150th anniversary to the erection of the church clock.

3. 110th anniversary of the recast front 3 bells & 7th bell by John Taylor & Co Bellfounders of Loughborough who at that time rehung the whole ring in a new cast iron H pattern bell frame mounted on rolled steel girders and provided all new fittings and dedicated on 22nd of December 1914 110 years ago tomorrow.

This QP was arranged by 5 to mark the 5th anniversary of the passing of the former tower captain, Ron Battams. The band was carefully selected so that it was made up of those who were members of the former Wednesday night practice at Aspley, or those who knew Ron. James Saunders was due to be part of this band, but was unwell. He would like to be associated with this performance, and thanks to Godfrey for stepping in.
Richard Lanyon-Hogg would also like to be associated with this performance, and has kindly written some words about Ron:
In Loving Memory of Ron Battams (5th June 1939 – 8th December 2019)

Tower Captain of St. Botolph’s, Aspley Guise, 1976–2019. A devoted ringer, teacher, and friend, Ron shared his wisdom, patience, and joy with all who knew him. Through decades of quiet, steadfast service, he was a pillar of strength in ever-changing times, dedicated to his church, his village, and the ringing tradition.

A true gentleman, Ron nurtured generations of ringers, guiding with kindness, humor, and an unerring sense of purpose. His legacy lives on, ringing out through the bells he loved and the countless lives he touched along the way.
“Ears, ears, ears” – his steady call still echoes in our hearts.
